summary: Describes obsolete syntax that IMAP4 implementations might meet when dealing with older versions of the Internet Mail Access Protocol. It is informational and meant to help with compatibility.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a dictionary of old words that older mail programs still use.

subtitle: Commands and responses no longer used in modern IMAP implementations

tldr.problem: As the Internet Message Access Protocol evolved, some early commands and responses became obsolete and were replaced with better alternatives, but older implementations might still use them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the obsolete syntax from earlier IMAP versions (RFC 1176 and RFC 1730) so newer implementations understand what old clients and servers might send.
tldr.outcome: IMAP4 implementations can choose to support these old commands for compatibility, but they are not required in new servers or clients.

today: RFC 2062 remains informational guidance for implementors. Modern IMAP4 servers are not required to support this obsolete syntax, but the document serves as a reference for those maintaining systems that need backward compatibility with old IMAP clients and servers from the 1990s.

sections.title: Purpose of Documenting Obsolete Syntax
sections.content:
RFC 2062 is a reference guide for implementors of IMAP4 who need to support older versions of the Internet Message Access Protocol. The RFC documents syntax that has become obsolete through the evolution of IMAP, drawing from RFC 1176 and RFC 1730. The primary goal is to help modern implementations achieve maximum interoperability with older IMAP clients and servers by explaining what legacy commands and responses they may encounter.

Modern servers are not required to implement any of this obsolete syntax, but the documentation exists for those who choose to support it for compatibility purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes old programs still use old commands. This document lists those old commands so new programs can understand them and talk to old programs.

sections.title: Obsolete Commands and Fetch Items
sections.content:
The RFC describes several commands that are no longer part of modern IMAP. FIND ALL.MAILBOXES returned mailbox names matching a pattern, with wildcards where percent (%) and question mark (?) matched single characters. FIND MAILBOXES did the same but only for mailboxes the user had marked as active or subscribed.

SUBSCRIBE MAILBOX and UNSUBSCRIBE MAILBOX were older forms of the SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE commands, using explicit MAILBOX keywords. The PARTIAL command allowed fetching only a portion of a message (starting at a specific octet position for a specific length), useful for downloading large messages over slow links.

Several obsolete FETCH data items are also documented: BODY[0] for the message header, RFC822.HEADER.LINES with selectable header fields, RFC822.PEEK variants, and their .NOT forms for excluding headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Old IMAP had commands like FIND to list mailboxes and PARTIAL to download only part of a message, which newer IMAP doesn't use anymore.

sections.title: Obsolete Server Responses
sections.content:
The MAILBOX response was sent by servers in reply to FIND commands, containing a single mailbox name that matched the search pattern. Servers must not send this response for any other reason, and client implementations that do not use FIND commands may safely ignore it.

The COPY response was returned in early experimental IMAP versions to confirm each message was copied successfully in response to a COPY command. New servers must never transmit it, and clients must ignore it if received from old servers.

The STORE response, also from experimental versions, was returned instead of FETCH to report the new value of flags after a STORE command. Clients should treat it identically to a FETCH response if encountered from legacy servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Old IMAP servers sent special messages like MAILBOX and COPY to confirm actions, but new mail programs don't expect those anymore.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC provides formal syntax definitions for all obsolete commands and responses using the same notation as the main IMAP specification. Each obsolete syntax rule is suffixed with "_old" (for example, command_auth_old adds the FIND command to the main authentication command set).

A unique aspect of older IMAP date handling is documented: the date_year_old syntax represents years as (year - 1900), and the date_time_old format uses a named time zone (like EST, UTC, or GMT) rather than numeric offsets. The RFC also defines all the historical time zone abbreviations used in early IMAP implementations.

These formal definitions allow implementors to write parsers that can correctly handle both old and new IMAP syntax when backward compatibility is desired.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows the exact rules for how old IMAP commands were written, so programmers can recognize them when old programs send them.
